purpose: Expand the reusable Biblical Scene registry with major narrative and visionary situations repeatedly used by the comparator.

scenes.title: Eden, expulsion and the guarded way to the Tree of Life
scenes.summary: Human life is placed in a cultivated garden containing the Tree of Life and the tree of knowledge. After transgression, the humans are expelled and cherubim with a turning flaming sword guard the way to the Tree of Life.
scenes.lead_in: Genesis 2 forms the human from the ground, gives life by breath and places the human in the garden to cultivate and keep it.
sequence: guarded way to Tree of Life
scenes.outcome: Access to life becomes a guarded boundary rather than an unrestricted condition.
scenes.what_follows: Genesis moves into life outside Eden, beginning with Cain and Abel and the expansion of human society and violence.
scenes.historical_context: The Eden narrative belongs to Israel's primeval-history traditions and uses ancient garden, divine-presence and mortality imagery.
scenes.literary_context: Genesis 2-3 moves from formation and vocation to boundary violation, mortality and exile from sacred space.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Later theological traditions read the scene in many ways; the text itself should remain distinct from later doctrines of original sin.
counterreadings_or_limits: The guarded way is east of Eden; it is not described as a North Pole gate.
Cherubim are guardians in the narrative, not modern human opponents.

scenes.title: Joseph is favored, rejected by his brothers, thrown into a pit and sold away
scenes.summary: Joseph's favored status, dreams and family tensions culminate in his brothers stripping his robe, throwing him into a pit and selling him to traders bound for Egypt while his father is led to believe he is dead.
scenes.setting: Jacob's household and the fields near Dothan
scenes.lead_in: Joseph is introduced as a favored son who reports dreams that imply future elevation over his family, intensifying existing resentment.
sequence: false death evidence shown to Jacob
scenes.outcome: The favored son is removed from the family and enters a downward foreign trajectory while being treated at home as effectively dead.
scenes.what_follows: Joseph serves in Potiphar's house, is falsely accused and is imprisoned before later elevation.
scenes.historical_context: The Joseph cycle is a literary family-and-diaspora narrative set within patriarchal traditions; details of social practice belong to an ancient Near Eastern setting.
scenes.literary_context: Genesis 37 opens the Joseph novella/cycle and establishes descent, hidden providence and family rupture that the later chapters reverse.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The narrative uses overlapping trader labels and complex source traditions; this does not change the central sold-away sequence.
counterreadings_or_limits: Modern rejection or online conflict is not equivalent to ancient enslavement.

scenes.title: Joseph is falsely accused, imprisoned and becomes attentive to other prisoners
scenes.summary: After prospering in Potiphar's household, Joseph rejects his master's wife's advances, is accused and imprisoned. In custody he gains responsibility, notices the distress of Pharaoh's officers and interprets their dreams.
scenes.setting: Egyptian household followed by royal prison/custody
scenes.lead_in: Joseph has risen from sold-away outsider to trusted household administrator before the accusation reverses his position.
scenes.outcome: Confinement becomes another site of service and interpretive competence, but Joseph remains forgotten for a time.
scenes.what_follows: Pharaoh dreams; the cupbearer remembers Joseph, initiating release and elevation.
scenes.historical_context: The narrative reflects an ancient story-world of household servitude, royal administration and prison; it should not be mapped directly onto modern legal institutions.
scenes.literary_context: Genesis 39-40 repeats the cycle's descent-and-favor pattern: Joseph is lowered by others yet receives responsibility within the lower state.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The story's moral and providential framing belongs to Genesis; modern innocence claims require independent evidence rather than typological transfer.
counterreadings_or_limits: Joseph's innocence in the story cannot establish innocence in an unrelated modern case.

scenes.title: Joseph is released, elevated over Pharaoh's house and builds grain infrastructure
scenes.summary: Joseph is summoned from confinement to interpret Pharaoh's dreams, is elevated over Egypt, organizes grain storage during abundance and later becomes the channel through which famine-stricken people and eventually his own family obtain food. He ultimately reveals himself to his brothers and interprets his descent through a preservation-of-life frame.
scenes.setting: Pharaoh's court, Egyptian administration and famine-era grain distribution
scenes.lead_in: After years of descent, household service and prison, Pharaoh's troubling dreams create a need for Joseph's interpretive skill.
scenes.outcome: The rejected/imprisoned son becomes an administrative preservation system and family reconciliation becomes possible.
scenes.what_follows: Jacob's household relocates to Egypt; Genesis eventually closes with Joseph's retrospective statement that intended harm was turned toward preserving many lives.
scenes.historical_context: The Joseph narrative imagines centralized royal food administration in Egypt; its literary-theological function is more certain than reconstructing exact historical institutions behind the story.
scenes.literary_context: Genesis 41-45 reverses the prior descent: pit/prison becomes court/house authority, scarcity becomes stored provision and hidden identity becomes recognition.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: Calling Joseph 'father to Pharaoh' in Genesis 45 is an honorific/functional statement within the narrative, not biological fatherhood.
counterreadings_or_limits: A modern claim to be a spiritual banker/provider is not validated merely by resemblance to Joseph.

scenes.title: Arrest, interrogation, condemnation and crucifixion in Mark's Passion
scenes.summary: After Gethsemane Jesus is arrested, questioned before Jewish authorities, denied by Peter, brought before Pilate, mocked, condemned and crucified. He dies and is placed in a tomb witnessed by followers.
scenes.setting: Gethsemane, Jerusalem authorities, Roman governor's proceedings, Golgotha and tomb
scenes.lead_in: Jesus enters Jerusalem amid escalating conflict, shares a final meal with disciples and predicts betrayal, scattering and denial.
scenes.outcome: Jesus' public ministry ends in Roman execution and burial, setting the narrative problem answered by the resurrection announcement in Mark 16.
scenes.what_follows: Women come to the tomb and encounter the announcement that Jesus has been raised.
scenes.historical_context: Crucifixion was a Roman execution practice. Gospel Passion narratives are theological narratives rooted in first-century Judean/Roman power structures, not descriptions of modern online humiliation.
scenes.literary_context: Mark's Passion resolves conflicts and predictions developed throughout the Gospel and immediately precedes the empty-tomb announcement.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The four Gospels differ in sequence, sayings and emphases; this scene follows Mark rather than creating a synthetic chronology.
counterreadings_or_limits: Metaphorical 'crucifixion' in a modern project is not historical Roman crucifixion.
Suffering or rejection alone does not establish messianic identity.

scenes.title: Thomas encounters the risen Jesus through wounds and recognition
scenes.summary: Jesus appears to disciples after the crucifixion, but Thomas is absent. Thomas says he requires contact with the wounds; at a later appearance Jesus invites him to inspect them, and Thomas responds with a climactic confession.
scenes.setting: disciples gathered behind closed doors after Jesus' death
scenes.lead_in: Mary Magdalene has encountered the risen Jesus and the disciples are gathered in fear; Thomas misses the first group appearance.
scenes.outcome: Wounds become part of post-death identity recognition rather than simply disappearing from the risen figure.
scenes.what_follows: John gives a purpose statement about signs and belief before an additional Galilee appearance in chapter 21.
scenes.historical_context: Thomas is one of the Twelve in the Gospel tradition; 'Didymus' means Twin, though the text does not identify a named twin sibling.
scenes.literary_context: The scene is a culminating Johannine recognition narrative, bringing signs, seeing, belief and Jesus' identity together.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The common label 'Doubting Thomas' simplifies a scene that ends in one of John's strongest confessions.
counterreadings_or_limits: The text does not identify a modern person called Thomas/Twin with the apostle or with Jesus.

scenes.title: One like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days
scenes.summary: Daniel sees violent beastly kingdoms rise from the sea, then a heavenly court with the Ancient of Days. One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives dominion, glory and kingdom, while the vision is also interpreted in relation to the holy ones receiving the kingdom.
participants: one like a son of man
scenes.setting: night vision moving from chaotic sea/earthly kingdoms to heavenly court
scenes.lead_in: Daniel has already interpreted imperial dreams; chapter 7 begins a sequence of Daniel's own symbolic visions.
sequence: one like son of man comes with clouds
interpretation connects kingdom with holy ones
scenes.outcome: Beastly imperial power is judged and human-like/heavenly kingship replaces it in a vision central to later Jewish and Christian Son-of-Man language.
scenes.what_follows: Daniel receives further visions about empires, conflict and restoration.
scenes.historical_context: Daniel 7 is apocalyptic resistance literature shaped by imperial crisis; scholarly interpretations debate the precise identity/corporate-individual relation of the human-like figure.
scenes.literary_context: The vision contrasts beastly empire with divinely judged and humanized rule, then interprets the kingdom in relation to the holy ones.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: 'Son of man' here is an Aramaic human-like expression within the vision; later Gospel usage develops the phrase in new contexts.
counterreadings_or_limits: Cloud imagery here is apocalyptic/theophanic, not cloud computing or literal mashed-food imagery.
The figure comes to the Ancient of Days within the vision; popular shorthand about direction should be checked against the text.

scenes.title: The Lion is announced, a slain-standing Lamb appears, and the scroll is opened
scenes.summary: John enters a heavenly throne vision and sees a sealed scroll that no one can open. An elder announces the victorious Lion of Judah and Root of David, but John sees a Lamb standing as though slain. The Lamb takes the scroll and receives worship because its death is interpreted as ransoming a people for God.
scenes.lead_in: After messages to seven churches, John sees an open door in heaven and is summoned into a throne-room vision.
sequence: heavenly worship interprets victory through sacrifice
scenes.outcome: Royal victory is disclosed through a paradoxical wounded Lamb who can open hidden judgment/history represented by the scroll.
scenes.what_follows: The Lamb opens the seals and Revelation's judgment visions advance.
scenes.historical_context: Revelation uses Jewish apocalyptic symbolism and imperial critique within late first-century Christian communities.
scenes.literary_context: The Lion/Lamb reversal is deliberate: what is announced as conquering royal power is visually disclosed as sacrificial, wounded yet standing power.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The symbolic figures should not be flattened into zoological or modern political identities.
counterreadings_or_limits: A modern use of Lion/Lamb titles is appropriation or comparison; it does not establish identity with Revelation's Christological figure.

scenes.title: Ezekiel's mobile throne vision: living creatures, wheels and Spirit-driven movement
scenes.summary: In exile Ezekiel sees a storm-like divine manifestation with four living creatures, intersecting wheels capable of movement in multiple directions, a radiant expanse and a throne-like structure above them. The vision culminates in the likeness of divine glory and Ezekiel falling down.
scenes.setting: among Judean exiles by the Chebar canal/river
scenes.lead_in: The book introduces Ezekiel as a priest among exiles when the heavens are opened and visions begin.
scenes.outcome: Divine presence is presented as mobile and not confined to Jerusalem; the vision inaugurates Ezekiel's prophetic commission.
scenes.what_follows: Ezekiel is commissioned to speak to a resistant people; related throne/wheel imagery returns in Ezekiel 10.
scenes.historical_context: The vision emerges in Babylonian exile, where divine mobility answers the crisis of distance from Jerusalem and temple.
scenes.literary_context: Ezekiel 1 establishes visual vocabulary reused throughout the book for divine presence, judgment and departure/return.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The famously difficult Hebrew imagery produces translation differences; 'wheel within a wheel' is visionary machinery, not a geometric proof of a specific modern object.
counterreadings_or_limits: The text does not describe a potato, UFO or Saturnian mechanism as its historical referent.

scenes.title: New Jerusalem descends: dwelling, open gates, river and Tree of Life
scenes.summary: John sees a new heaven and earth and the holy city New Jerusalem descending from God. Divine dwelling is with humanity; death and mourning are overcome. The city has measured gates and foundations but no temple building, because God and the Lamb are its temple. A river of life flows from the throne and the Tree of Life bears fruit for the healing of nations.
scenes.setting: vision of renewed creation and descending holy city
scenes.lead_in: Revelation 20 concludes judgment imagery; chapter 21 turns toward renewed creation and restored divine-human dwelling.
scenes.outcome: The Bible's final city image transforms exile and guarded-life motifs into restored dwelling, access, healing and shared presence.
scenes.what_follows: Revelation concludes with testimony, invitation, warnings about the book and expectation of coming.
scenes.historical_context: New Jerusalem draws on prophetic restoration, temple and Zion traditions while addressing communities living within Roman imperial reality.
scenes.literary_context: The ending deliberately echoes Genesis: Tree and river imagery return, while curse, death and exclusion are reconfigured within a restored city.
scenes.textual_or_translation_caveats: The city's measurements and materials belong to apocalyptic symbolism; interpretive traditions differ over literal, ecclesial and eschatological readings.
counterreadings_or_limits: Revelation does not locate New Jerusalem at the geographic North Pole.
The city descends from heaven; it is not identical to Jacob's stairway.
